clubHeadline: A smaller head tells you more. Roll it pure.
clubParas: A milled blade for the player who wants the truth about every putt. One block of 431 stainless, so the strike comes back muted and solid with no ping. 385 grams, heavy for a blade, and planted on a four-footer when the hands want to help. You feel exactly where on the face you hit it.

clubSpecs.v: Blade putter, CNC-milled from a single block of 431 stainless.
Muted and solid at impact. No ring, no ping, no buzz through the hands, and honest feedback on the ones you miss.
One-piece 431 stainless head, milled face, 3.5° of loft and 385 g at 35 inches. Gold finish, Lucky rubber grip.
Players who release the head through the stroke and want to know about a miss, not have it covered up.

videoBrief: 16:9 product film, 40–60s. Down-the-line showing the arc the head wants to travel on, then the face at impact in slow motion. A blade's argument is feel, which is the hardest thing to film. Lean on sound.

look.photo: Bold, full-bleed, portrait. Blade head at address on the green, low sun along the top line. Shot from the golfer's eyeline so the small head reads as small. That is the appeal.
look.headline: Less club, more information
paras: A blade is the smallest thing you will look down at all round, and every miss tells you about itself. Either that is why you play one, or it is why you don't.
In gold, at 385 grams, it is also the least apologetic putter we make.
If you would rather the head covered the miss, the Tracer Mallet is the other one.

helpPick.headline: Both suit an arc. The question is feel or forgiveness.
helpPick.sub: This is the only question worth asking about a putter and the usual answer (mallets for straight strokes, blades for arcs) does not apply here. Both Tracers are built for a stroke with a natural arc. What separates them is how much the head helps you on the ones you miss, and how much it tells you about them.

options.name: Tracer Blade
options.body: For players who release the head through the stroke. Twenty grams heavier and far less forgiving. The trade is that a blade tells you exactly where on the face you hit it.

options.name: Tracer Mallet
options.body: Slight toe hang from a plumber neck, so it works with the arc you already have. Perimeter weighting keeps an off-center strike on line. You give up some feedback to get that.

helpPick.note: The blade is out of stock and right hand only when it returns. If you want the feedback rather than the forgiveness, that is worth waiting for.

_club: Rewritten 2026-08-19 under Cole's rule: bold, in Lucky's vocabulary, AND one thing per line, said once, no commentary. The headline stays (Cole: 'I didn't think that was bad'). The body stops circling: ~45-50 words, the club named in the first line, facts paired with what they deliver, zero self-reference, zero 'and that is the point' / 'which is exactly why'. The Gold's intro is the model Cole approved ('perfect, you nailed it'). SECOND PASS same day: Cole caught the body drifting back to long three-clause sentences with no culture vocabulary. The Gold's pattern, exactly: short sentences, each one spec -> what it does, the golf word in it.

clubGrinds.v: A blade will not straighten out a strike you missed. It tells you what you did instead. For players who release the head through the stroke.

clubGrinds.k: The grip: nothing in the way
clubGrinds.v: The stock Lucky rubber grip, not the oversized 3.0 on the mallet. An arcing stroke wants to feel the club, and a fat grip takes that away.

_specTabs: Takomo-shaped 2026-08-19 to match the Gold: three cards (Clubs / Shafts / Grips), each a caption, a stacked key/value head and a black-header matrix. A putter has one loft and one length, so the Clubs matrix runs the four figures as COLUMNS against one head-shape row rather than lofts as columns. The old shape was Club / Shaft & grip. specSub used to name "the Product Reference Guide v1.8" in customer-facing text: an internal document and its version number, on the page.
